system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Multi-agent graph exploration
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Barrier-based traps showing Ω(log log n) agents are needed when each agent has sublogarithmic memory. Also the matching O(log log n) upper bound that uses agent configurations as boosted virtual memory.

ATOMS:
- CS-ALG-C07-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: A k-barrier B_k for an algorithm A in a graph G is a subgraph whose removal disconnects G into two connected components, such that no agent ever traverses B_k from one component to the other without at least k other agents entering B_k during the traversal.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0173-s22] A k-barrier Bk in a graph G for an algorithm A is a subgraph of G whose removal disconnects the graph into two connected components, with the property that no agent ever traverses Bk from one component to the other without at least k other agents entering Bk during the traversal.
- CS-ALG-C07-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: Multi-agent exploration uses k ≥ 2 deterministic, distinguishable agents that each behave as individual agents, move in a synchronized fashion, and may exchange information while co-located at a vertex.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0173-s09] More precisely, we con- sider a setting with k ≥2 deterministic and distinguishable agents that behave as before individually, but move in a synchronized fashion and may exchange information while co-located at a vertex.
- CS-ALG-C07-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: A 1-barrier plays the role of a simultaneous trap for every individual agent.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0173-s23] In particular, a 1-barrier plays the role of a simultaneous trap for every individual agent.
- CS-ALG-C07-S2-01.r1 | S3
  ATOM: Deterministic exploration of undirected graphs of size $n$ requires at least $\Omega(\log\log n)$ agents if each agent is allowed only $O(\log^{1-\varepsilon} n)$ bits of memory, where $\varepsilon>0$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0174-s27] Deterministic exploration of undirected graphs needs at least Ω(loglogn) agents if we allow O(log1−ε n) bits of memory for every agent, where ε > 0.
- CS-ALG-C07-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: Undirected graphs can be deterministically explored with $O(\log\log n)$ agents, even if each agent is allowed only constant memory.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0175-s24] Undirected graphs can be deterministically explored with O (loglogn) agents, even if we only allow constant memory for every agent.
- CS-ALG-C07-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: A constant number a of distinguishable agents placed along a cycle T yields |T|^a configurations. These configurations act as virtual memory of m_1 = log |T|^a bits, which is of order a·m_0 and so boosts the memory capacity by roughly a factor of a.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0175-s12] Since agents are distinguishable, there are |T|a conﬁgurations that can be established in this way.
    [CS-ALG-p0175-s14] The number of memory bits that can be encoded in this way is m1 = log|T|a, which is of order am0.
- CS-ALG-C07-S3-01.r1a | S2
  ATOM: As the number of vertices $n$ increases, the number of such agent configurations grows as $n^k$, so configurations can no longer be expected to ever repeat.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0173-s18] As we increase the number of vertices n, the number of such conﬁgurations grows as nk, and we can no longer hope for conﬁgurations to ever repeat.
- CS-ALG-C07-S3-01.r1b | S2
  ATOM: Forcing the agents to stay "close" to each other keeps the number of configurations bounded, which allows the same general approach as before to be used.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0173-s19] The key idea to overcome this is to force the agents to stay “close” to each other, which ensures that the number of conﬁgurations stays bounded and allows us to use the same general approach as before.
- CS-ALG-C07-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: O(log n) agents are trivially sufficient for exploration, because agents can move together and each can maintain a constant number of the memory bits that Reingold's algorithm needs.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0175-s04] Observe that O (logn) agents are trivially sufﬁcient by Reingold’s algorithm (Theorem 2), since we can let agents move together and make each one responsible for maintaining a constant num- ber of memory bits.
- CS-ALG-C07-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: The recursive virtual-memory upper bound only works if each recursion level needs just a constant number of agents and memory bits, both to encode and to manipulate the virtual memory.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0175-s19] For this approach to yield the claimed bound, it is crucial to argue that only a con- stant number of agents and memory bits are needed in each recursive level, not only to encode, but also to manipulate the virtual memory.
- CS-ALG-C07-S3-04 | S3
  ATOM: The $\Omega(\log\log n)$ lower bound applies only to sublogarithmic memory, because $O(\log n)$ agents are trivially sufficient. Agents can move together, each maintaining a constant number of the bits that Reingold's algorithm needs.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0175-s04] Observe that O (logn) agents are trivially sufﬁcient by Reingold’s algorithm (Theorem 2), since we can let agents move together and make each one responsible for maintaining a constant num- ber of memory bits.
